title: Biased random generator
label: idb
statement:
Input:

getRandom01Biased()

Returns 0 with probability p
Returns 1 with probability (1-p)

Output:

getRandom06Uniform()

Returns an integer from [0,6] with uniform probability.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Input:
> 
> getRandom01Biased()
> 
> Returns 0 with probability p
> Returns 1 with probability (1-p)
> 
> Output:
> 
> getRandom06Uniform()
> 
> Returns an integer from [0,6] with uniform probability.

You have one source of randomness and it is unfair. You need seven equally likely outcomes out of it. Nothing about the source can be changed, and its bias may be unknown.

A single integer in 0..6, with each of the seven values having probability exactly 1/7.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
Is `p` known? The signature says only that the generator is biased, not by how much.

This matters, and the good answer does not need to know. **A solution that works for unknown p is strictly better than one that uses it**, and Von Neumann debiasing never refers to p at all. If p were known you could do better on the expected number of calls — arithmetic coding gets close to the entropy bound — but you would have bought a small constant factor with a dependency on a value that is usually only approximately known. Say that you are deliberately not using p.

One thing does have to be assumed: `0 < p < 1`. If p is 0 or 1 the source has no entropy and no algorithm can produce a fair bit from it.

| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| Successive calls are independent. | The whole construction relies on it. If the source were correlated — say it alternated — pairing two draws would produce a **deterministic** result, not a fair bit. Worth saying, because it is the one assumption that cannot be worked around. |
| p is fixed across calls. | If the bias drifts, the pairing argument still holds **within** a pair but the expected cost changes over time. Correctness survives; performance predictions do not. |
| `0 < p < 1`. | At the extremes the source is a constant and the task is impossible. Stating it is a one-line acknowledgement that you know where the method’s domain ends. |
| Unbounded worst-case time is acceptable. | If it is not, no exact method exists. You would have to accept a tiny bias with a call cap, which is a legitimate engineering trade and should be named as one. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
There are two separate problems here and conflating them is what makes this question hard. **Solve them one at a time.**

*Problem one: remove the bias.* Call the source twice. The outcome `01` has probability `p(1-p)`. The outcome `10` has probability `(1-p)p`. Multiplication commutes, so **those two are exactly equal whatever p is**. The other two outcomes, `00` and `11`, are the ones carrying the bias — so throw them away and draw again. Return the first bit of any pair that disagrees, and you have a perfectly fair bit from a source whose bias you never measured. That is Von Neumann’s trick, and the whole of it is the observation that `p(1-p) = (1-p)p`.

*Problem two: get seven outcomes from fair bits.* Three fair bits give eight equally likely values, 0 through 7. You want seven. Eight does not divide by seven, so **no mapping of the eight onto the seven can be uniform** — some value would have to receive two of the eight, making it twice as likely. The only correct move is to **reject**: if the three bits give 7, discard them and draw three more. This is rejection sampling, and the temptation it defeats is `value % 7`, which is wrong and looks fine.

Both halves are the same idea applied twice: *when the outcomes you have do not divide evenly into the outcomes you want, discard rather than squeeze.* Neither half needs to know p, and neither has a bounded worst case — both facts are worth stating rather than hoping nobody asks.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** Call the source three times, treat the bits as a binary number, take it modulo 7. *O(1) calls, O(1) space, and **wrong**.*

**Why not good enough.** Two independent errors, and being able to name both is the point of the question. First, the bits are biased, so the eight patterns are not equally likely to begin with — `000` has probability p³ and `111` has `(1-p)³`. Second, even with perfectly fair bits, `% 7` maps both 0 and 7 onto 0, so 0 would come out twice as often as everything else. The second error survives fixing the first, which is why the modulo shortcut is worth explicitly rejecting out loud.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | `Func<int> biasedBit` returning 0 with probability p, 1 with probability 1−p |
| TRANSFORMATION | Pairs of draws → a fair bit, by keeping only the two outcomes that are equally likely by symmetry |
| DATA STRUCTURE | None. Two local integers. |
| ALGORITHM | Debias to a fair bit; take three fair bits as a value in 0..7; reject 7 and redraw |
| OUTPUT | A uniform integer in 0..6 |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- `FairBit()`: draw two bits. If they differ, return the first. If they match, repeat.
- `Next0To6()`: build `v = (b₂ << 2) | (b₁ << 1) | b₀` from three fair bits.
- If `v <= 6`, return it. Otherwise discard all three bits and start again.

- **Exactly** uniform, not approximately. Any scheme that maps an unequal number of source outcomes onto the seven values is wrong, however small the error looks.
- The number of calls to the source is not fixed. Any exact method must be able to give up and retry.
- Seven is not a power of two, which is the second difficulty and is independent of the bias.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| No data structure at all | Worth saying, because "reach for a structure" is the reflex this question punishes. The entire solution is two loops and a shift. |
| Pairs, not triples or longer runs | Pairs are the smallest window in which two distinct outcomes have provably equal probability. Longer windows admit more accepted patterns and are more efficient — that is the advanced-extraction follow-up — but pairs are the ones you can prove on a whiteboard in one line. |
| Three fair bits, not a loop up to 7 | Three bits is the smallest power of two above seven, so it wastes the least. Two bits cannot reach 6 at all. |
| Rejection, not modulo or scaling | The only exactly uniform option. Everything else trades a bounded call count for a bias, and the bias is the thing the question is about. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**`if (a != b) return a;` — why returning the first bit is correct.** The two accepted patterns are `01` and `10`, with equal probability. Returning the first bit returns 0 for one and 1 for the other, so each comes out half the time. Returning the **second** bit would be equally correct, inverted. What would not be correct is returning `a` on a match, which is where the bias lives.

**Why the outer loop discards all three bits.** On rejecting 7 the code loops and calls `FairBit()` three fresh times. Reusing two of the three — say keeping the top bits and redrawing the last — would correlate successive outputs, because the surviving bits are conditioned on having been part of a rejected triple. The conditioning is easy to miss and it is a real bug.

**Why `BiasedCalls` is instrumented.** It makes the expected cost measurable rather than asserted. The test compares the observed ratio against `24 / (7p(1-p))` at four values of p. In an interview I would not write the counter, but I would state the formula — and having actually measured it is why I am willing to state it.

**The clock on the wall: termination.** Both loops terminate with probability 1 and neither has a worst-case bound. For any `0 < p < 1` the accept probability per pair is `2p(1-p) > 0`, so the number of attempts is geometric with finite mean. "Terminates almost surely" is the honest phrase; "O(1)" is not.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FairBit` | expected 1/(p(1−p)) draws | O(1) | Each pair accepts with probability 2p(1−p); expected pairs is the reciprocal |
| `Next0To6` | expected 24/(7p(1−p)) draws | O(1) | 3 fair bits × 8/7 for the rejection × 2 draws per pair |
| worst case | unbounded | O(1) | Rejection sampling has no upper bound on attempts |

**At p = 0.5 that formula gives 13.7 biased calls per output, and the measured value is 13.7.** At p = 0.05 it predicts 72 and measures 72. The cost blows up as p approaches 0 or 1, because `p(1-p)` is the accept rate and it goes to zero — which is the honest answer to "how slow can this get".

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| p = 0 or p = 1 | The source is constant, every pair matches, and `FairBit` never returns. No algorithm can extract entropy that is not there — the right response is to state the precondition, not to add a retry limit that silently returns a wrong answer. |
| p very close to 0 or 1 | Correct but slow: cost scales as 1/(p(1−p)). At p = 0.001 that is roughly 3,400 draws per output. |
| Correlated source | Breaks correctness, not just speed. An alternating source makes every pair differ, so `FairBit` becomes deterministic. This is the assumption to state. |
| A range that **is** a power of two, say [0,7] | The outer rejection disappears entirely and the cost drops by 8/7. Worth mentioning as the reason seven is awkward. |
| Needing many values at once | Generate them independently. Batching does not help the fair-bit extraction, but advanced extractors do — see the follow-up. |

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Assuming the bias is known.

**Verification exercise:** Incorrect assumption — Sums of two dice are not uniform, and mod 10 does not fix it. Enumerating all 49 pairs gives counts **5 4 4 4 4 4 5 6 7 6** for outputs 1–10 — 9 comes up 7 times in 49, 2 only 4: 75% more likely.

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**Generalise it to [0, n-1] for any n.**

Take `b = ceil(log2(n))` fair bits, giving a value in `0 .. 2^b - 1`. Reject anything `>= n` and redraw all b bits. Accept probability is `n / 2^b`, which is always greater than 1/2, so the expected number of retries is under 2 regardless of n.

*Trade-off:* Simple and exact. The efficiency varies with how close n is to a power of two: n = 9 needs 4 bits and wastes 7 of 16 patterns, so it retries nearly half the time. A batched scheme that generates several values from one larger draw recovers most of that waste, at the cost of state between calls.

**Von Neumann throws away most of its input. Can you do better?**

Advanced extractors (Peres, or Elias’s method) recurse on the discarded information: the sequence of "was this pair a match" and "was the match 00 or 11" are two further biased sources to extract from. Peres’s iterated construction approaches the Shannon entropy bound, so at p = 0.5 you approach one fair bit per input bit rather than one per four.

*Trade-off:* Von Neumann is four lines and provably fair. Peres is recursive, needs buffering, and is much harder to convince a reviewer of. I would ship Von Neumann unless the source were genuinely expensive — a hardware entropy source, say — and then I would use a library, not my own implementation. The interview answer is to name the direction and the trade, not to write it.

**p is known. Does that change your answer?**

With p known you can do arithmetic coding on the source and approach the entropy bound directly, which is a large constant-factor win at extreme p. You could also pick pairing windows to maximise the accept rate.

*Trade-off:* p is almost never known **exactly** — it is measured, and it drifts. A method whose *correctness* depends on p is fragile in a way that a method whose only *speed* depends on p is not. Von Neumann is exactly uniform for every p in (0,1), including p values you measured wrongly. I would keep it unless profiling proved the source was the bottleneck.

**Now the reverse: given a uniform generator, produce outcomes with given weights.**

Build the prefix sums of the weights once, draw a uniform value in `[0, total)`, and binary-search for the first prefix sum strictly greater than it. O(n) to build, O(log n) per draw. The alias method gets O(1) per draw with O(n) preprocessing if draws vastly outnumber builds.

*Trade-off:* Prefix sums plus binary search is the answer to give: simple, and the preprocessing/query split is the same argument as Q11 and Q13. Mention the alias method as the O(1) option rather than implementing it.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *What are the edge cases — empty, duplicates, missing values, invalid input?* — Names them and says what the code does for each

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Time and space complexity? Can it be improved? What happens as N grows?* — States both, names the bottleneck
